info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 2.3: Auditing AI-Generated Manuscript Metadata.

name.text: 01 Question: What Today Actually Asks of You

questiontext.text: The workshop asks for at least two SUBTLE hallucinations. What makes an error subtle rather than obvious?

generalfeedback.text: The workshop asks you to name at least two subtle hallucinations, meaning errors that pass validation, so today trains you to audit a header that already looks perfect.

answer.text: It survives every automatic check: well-formed, schema-valid, correctly formatted, plausible — and still wrong.

feedback.text: Correct. An error the schema catches is one the machine already told you about, which earns little credit.

answer.text: It is small in scope, such as a single wrong character in an attribute value.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Subtlety is about escaping detection, not about size; a one-digit error in an identifier can be very subtle.

answer.text: It appears only in the physDesc section rather than the fileDesc.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Subtle errors can occur anywhere; location is not what defines them.

answer.text: It is an error the model admits to when asked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models do not reliably report their own errors, and an admitted error would not be hard to find.

name.text: 02 Question: Creating Your AI Accounts

questiontext.text: You are getting set up before the lab. Which statement correctly matches the accounts to the tools and states the caution the lesson attaches to hosted models?

generalfeedback.text: Set up one working AI account before the lab, check for student or academic access first, and decide what you are willing to paste into a hosted model — because training terms and rights restrictions both bite here.

answer.text: GitHub for Copilot, Google for Gemini and Antigravity, Anthropic for Claude Code, and OpenAI for Codex — and before pasting your own notes, ask whether the text is public and whether the tool trains on your input.

feedback.text: Correct. Each vendor's tool needs that vendor's account, and rights restrictions plus training terms together govern what you may paste into a hosted model.

answer.text: One GitHub account covers all four tools, since Copilot, Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity all run inside VS Code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Claude Code is Anthropic's, Codex is OpenAI's, and Antigravity is Google's; running in or alongside an editor does not make them one vendor's products.

answer.text: Any account will do because these tools are free to students, so there is no need to check each vendor's current academic terms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Free and education terms vary by vendor and change over time; the lesson says to check the vendor's current page and ask if you are unsure whether you qualify.

answer.text: Public catalogue records are always safe to paste, and free tiers never train on the text you enter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Free tiers frequently do train on input, and even a public text requires you to check the tool's training terms before pasting.

name.text: 03 Question: The AI Extensions for VS Code

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes the four AI coding tools discussed in this section?

generalfeedback.text: Copilot, Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are four different tools — three extend VS Code and one replaces it — and any of them will serve, so choose on which account you can actually get.

answer.text: Copilot offers inline completion inside a VS Code extension, while Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are agentic; Antigravity differs again because it is a standalone editor built on VS Code rather than an extension.

feedback.text: Correct. The two distinctions are completion versus agency and extension versus environment: three tools extend VS Code, and Antigravity replaces it.

answer.text: All four are VS Code extensions, and the only real difference is which vendor supplies the underlying model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Antigravity is a separate application built on VS Code, not an extension you add to it; choosing it means working in a different editor.

answer.text: Copilot is the agentic tool, while Claude Code and Codex merely complete the next line as you type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This inverts the distinction: Copilot began as completion, and Claude Code and Codex are the agentic tools you hand a task to.

answer.text: Antigravity is Google's VS Code extension for Gemini, so it runs inside the editor you have already configured for XML validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a standalone, agent-first editor built on VS Code; adopting it means configuring a second working environment.

name.text: 04 Question: What the Model Is Doing When It Writes Your Header

questiontext.text: A model predicts what usually comes next. What does that imply about where its description of your witness will be weakest?

generalfeedback.text: A model writes TEI by predicting what usually comes next, which makes it fluent, unable to check itself, and systematically wrong about whatever is distinctive in your witness.

answer.text: Wherever your manuscript is unusual, since the model supplies the usual answer regardless.

feedback.text: Correct. It produces the average manuscript, and your witness is not average.

answer.text: In the sections it has seen least often, such as the publicationStmt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common containers are handled well; the difficulty is unusual content, not unusual elements.

answer.text: At the end of the file, where prediction errors accumulate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Errors do not compound positionally in that way.

answer.text: Only in the attributes, since element names are easier to predict.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are predicted the same way, and factual errors appear in element content too.

name.text: 05 Question: Two Ways of Being Right

questiontext.text: How do a schema and a language model differ in the kind of correctness each delivers?

generalfeedback.text: Schemas are consistent but indifferent to meaning, models grasp meaning but guarantee nothing, so each covers the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is consistent but indifferent to meaning; the model grasps meaning but guarantees nothing.

feedback.text: Correct. They fail in opposite directions, so each covers the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is more accurate in every respect, so the model adds nothing to the workflow.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema cannot read messy prose and find meaning in it; a model genuinely can.

answer.text: Both are deterministic, but the schema runs faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model is probabilistic and may answer the same prompt differently twice.

answer.text: The model checks facts while the schema checks structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model does not check facts at all; it predicts them.

name.text: 06 Question: What a Schema Can and Cannot See

questiontext.text: Your file validates at zero errors. What has that certified, and what do you still need before you can audit an AI header?

generalfeedback.text: A schema certifies that a file is well built, never that it is true, and every fact about the physical manuscript falls outside what it can see. Your verified header is what converts an impression of the AI's cleverness into a specific, checkable claim about what it got wrong.

answer.text: It certifies only that the file is well built; auditing still requires your own verified header as an independent reference, without which you can report impressions but not checkable claims.

feedback.text: Correct. The schema is blind to every fact about the physical manuscript, and your Tuesday header is the ground truth the AI output is measured against.

answer.text: That the file describes the manuscript accurately, and that no independent reference is therefore needed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema checks that values are of permitted types, never whether a shelfmark, date, or material is the right one.

answer.text: That the file is well built and factually consistent with its sources, so the AI output can be audited against the schema alone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Source consistency is outside what a schema can see; without your own verified header you have no independent standard.

answer.text: That the file will import into Moodle without error, which is enough to compare the AI output against the schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Import compatibility is not validity, and neither certifies truth; the comparison needs your own verified header as the reference.

name.text: 07 Question: Finding the Information: Where Your Facts Come From

questiontext.text: Before generating an AI header, why must you assemble a verified dossier on your own document?

generalfeedback.text: Build a verified dossier — object identity, physical description, responsible agents and places, and textual content — before generating anything, because you cannot audit the machine against facts you never established.

answer.text: Because you cannot audit the machine against facts you never established yourself.

feedback.text: Correct. The comparison is only possible if you hold verified values independently of the model.

answer.text: Because the model requires structured input to produce valid XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model will produce valid-looking XML from almost any input; the dossier exists for your audit, not its convenience.

answer.text: Because authority registers will not accept requests without a shelfmark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Registers are searchable by name and other fields; no dossier is required to query them.

answer.text: Because the schema validates the dossier rather than the header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema validates the XML header; the dossier is your reference material.

name.text: 08 Question: Recording What You Found in the Header

questiontext.text: You are describing a document whose surviving exemplar is a printed proclamation with no original. How should the header record that?

generalfeedback.text: Put each fact in the element whose meaning actually fits it — typed ``, `ref` on the identified element, an accurate `@form`, status in a `` — and record uncertainty rather than concealing it.

answer.text: In a <note> stating the object's status, because a reference number alone does not say whether you hold an original, a copy, or a print.

feedback.text: Correct. Without it a reader will assume an original, which is exactly the error to avoid.

answer.text: By omitting the identifier, since no original means nothing to cite.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The surviving exemplar is precisely what you cite; the absence of an original is information about it.

answer.text: By using @n on <msItem> to mark it as a copy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @n numbers items within a manuscript; it does not record the object's status.

answer.text: In the <publicationStmt>, since printing is a publication act.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <publicationStmt> describes your edition, not the historical object.

name.text: 09 Question: Choosing the Right Element for the Right Fact

questiontext.text: You are cataloguing a single-sheet printed broadside. Why is <handDesc> the wrong element for it?

generalfeedback.text: Choose the element whose meaning actually matches your object, use the categories that honestly apply, and record the misfit in a note rather than forcing a category that asserts something untrue.

answer.text: A printed document has no scribal hands, so asserting one states something false about the object — and no schema will stop you.

feedback.text: Correct. The schema permits the element; only your knowledge of the object tells you it does not apply.

answer.text: Because <handDesc> is not permitted inside <physDesc>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is permitted there, which is exactly why the error survives validation.

answer.text: Because printed documents require <decoDesc> instead.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Decoration is a separate matter; the issue is that hands do not apply at all.

answer.text: Because the schema's enumeration of hands excludes printed work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such enumeration; the mismatch is conceptual, not schema-enforced.

name.text: 10 Question: What Your Dossier Must Cover Before You Generate

questiontext.text: Your dossier has a field you could not verify from any source. What should you do with it?

generalfeedback.text: Assemble a sourced dossier covering object, physical form, content, agents, places, and date before generating — marking what you could not verify, because unmarked gaps are where fabrication hides.

answer.text: Mark it explicitly as unverified, rather than omitting it silently.

feedback.text: Correct. An omission you know about is safe; a forgotten one is where the machine's invention goes unnoticed.

answer.text: Omit it, so the AI cannot reproduce a wrong value.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting it removes your ability to notice when the model invents something for that field.

answer.text: Fill it with the most likely value and check it later.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That seeds your own fabrication into the ground truth you will audit against.

answer.text: Include it and let the schema flag it as uncertain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema has no way to represent or detect uncertainty about a fact.

name.text: 11 Question: Working With a Model That Cannot See Your Document

questiontext.text: A model has never handled a physical manuscript. Where will its description be weakest?

generalfeedback.text: A model's knowledge comes from descriptions rather than objects, so its failures cluster on facts requiring physical access or a queryable register — which is exactly the ground your dossier covers.

answer.text: On facts requiring physical access or a queryable register — hand counts, dimensions, condition, shelfmarks.

feedback.text: Correct. Those are exactly the fields your dossier covers and the schema cannot check.

answer.text: On long descriptive prose, where it loses coherence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fluent prose is its strength; the failures are factual, not stylistic.

answer.text: On rare TEI elements it has seen infrequently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structural markup is what it has read most about, and what the schema checks.

answer.text: On dates, because calendars are arithmetically complex.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It handles date formats well; it fails on the date the specific object actually carries.

name.text: 12 Question: Getting AI to Draft a Header Element

questiontext.text: Why does this section insist on prompting for one element at a time rather than asking the model for the whole <msDesc>?

generalfeedback.text: Prompt for one element at a time with your own verified facts, check it against your dossier before it enters the file, and validate after it does — small enough to verify is the rule.

answer.text: A whole-file request hides its errors inside a large plausible block, while a single element is small enough to check against your dossier in seconds — and it keeps you knowing what each line does.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why the loop is: ask for one element using verified facts, check it against the dossier, validate once it is in the file, and keep the correction.

answer.text: Because the model cannot produce a valid <msDesc> in a single response.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It produces one readily; the problem is that a whole-file answer is impressive and hard to verify, not that it is impossible.

answer.text: Because the schema will only validate one element at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema validates the whole file; the one-element rule is about making the output checkable, not about what the validator accepts.

answer.text: Because asking for one element is faster and uses fewer tokens.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is verifiability, not speed; the same mistake can recur, so you must understand why the element was wrong.

name.text: 13 Question: Asking the Model for a Header

questiontext.text: What should your prompt to the model contain?

generalfeedback.text: Prompt with real source material and the schema, withhold the answers, and save the model's output unedited so the comparison measures the machine rather than your corrections.

answer.text: Your raw source material and the schema requirement, with the correct answers withheld.

feedback.text: Correct. Withholding them is what makes the comparison measure the machine rather than your corrections.

answer.text: Your finished header, so the model can produce a matching version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That measures reproduction, not extraction; the audit becomes meaningless.

answer.text: Only the element names, so the model cannot be misled by detail.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Without source material it has nothing to extract and will invent everything.

answer.text: Your header plus a list of its errors, so the model can fix them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That measures the model plus your supervision, and destroys the baseline.

name.text: 14 Question: Holding Both to the Same Gate

questiontext.text: You run the validator on the AI output. Why must you record the error count before fixing anything?

generalfeedback.text: Validate the AI header unedited and record its raw error count before any repair, because that first number is the measurement and everything after it is remediation.

answer.text: Because that first count is the measurement, and everything after it is remediation.

feedback.text: Correct. Repair without a recorded baseline measures nothing about the model.

answer.text: Because the schema may report different errors on a second run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation is deterministic; the same file yields the same result.

answer.text: Because the count determines your workshop grade directly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The count is evidence for your comparison, not a score in itself.

answer.text: Because fixing errors first makes the file too large to validate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File size is irrelevant to validation.

name.text: 15 Question: The Audit: Comparing Content, Not Just Structure

questiontext.text: The AI produced a well-formed shelfmark that is simply false, and it passed validation. How should you mark it?

generalfeedback.text: Audit the machine field by field against your verified dossier, count both the schema errors and the wrong-or-invented fields, and be able to name the specific falsehood rather than a general impression of error.

answer.text: Invented — a confident, valid, false value counts as invented, and the schema passing it is the point.

feedback.text: Correct. This is the single most important category in the audit.

answer.text: Wrong, but only worth a partial deduction since the format is correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Correct formatting of a false value is what makes it dangerous, not what excuses it.

answer.text: Acceptable, since the schema is the agreed standard of correctness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema is the agreed standard of construction, not of truth.

answer.text: Missing, because the correct value was never supplied to the model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It supplied a value; the value is false, which is invention rather than omission.

name.text: 16 Question: Four Kinds of Wrong

questiontext.text: Why does the four-part classification of AI errors matter for your audit?

generalfeedback.text: AI errors are structural, obviously factual, subtly factual, or citational, and the categories differ by who is capable of catching them.

answer.text: The categories differ in who is capable of catching them, and only the harder ones demonstrate editorial skill.

feedback.text: Correct. A submission reporting two structural errors has reported what the machine already announced.

answer.text: The categories differ in how much they affect schema validity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Two of the four categories have no effect on validity at all.

answer.text: The categories determine which errors the model can repair itself.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Self-repair applies to structural errors regardless of the classification's purpose.

answer.text: The categories correspond to the four sections of the TEI header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They classify kinds of error, not locations in the file.

name.text: 17 Question: Structural Errors: The Ones the Schema Hands You

questiontext.text: Why are structural hallucinations the least valuable finding to report in your workshop comparison?

generalfeedback.text: Structural hallucinations are plausible, illegal markup that the schema catches instantly, which makes them the least valuable finding in your audit.

answer.text: The schema catches them automatically, so reporting them demonstrates nothing the machine did not already tell you.

feedback.text: Correct. They are worth counting, but the analysis has to go further to earn credit.

answer.text: They occur too rarely to make a convincing argument.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are common; commonness is not the issue.

answer.text: They are usually introduced by your own editing rather than the model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are the model's errors, present in the untouched output.

answer.text: They cannot be quoted in a written comparison.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They quote easily; the problem is that they are trivially detected.

name.text: 18 Question: Obvious Factual Errors: Check These First

questiontext.text: Models drift toward the famous when describing an unfamiliar manuscript. What auditing strategy follows?

generalfeedback.text: Obvious factual errors cluster in support, extent, hands, date, and repository, and models drift toward the famous, so check whatever is distinctive about your witness first.

answer.text: Check whatever is distinctive about your witness first, because that is where the average manuscript was substituted for yours.

feedback.text: Correct. Ordinary features are described well; unusual ones are where substitution happens.

answer.text: Check the most common fields first, since those are where most errors occur.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common fields are where the model performs best.

answer.text: Check the longest elements first, since more text means more opportunity for error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not what predicts error; distinctiveness is.

answer.text: Check the fields the schema flagged, since factual errors cluster near structural ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Factual errors are independent of where structural errors appear.

name.text: 19 Question: The Subtle One: The Provenance That Never Happened

questiontext.text: A model invents a transfer to the Provincial Archives in 1878, complete with an accession register, in valid TEI that passes at zero errors. What should you conclude from how specific it is?

generalfeedback.text: A model produces fabricated provenance in flawless TEI that passes the schema at zero errors, and its specificity is a warning sign rather than a mark of research.

answer.text: Specificity is a warning sign rather than evidence, since the model cannot be vague and a probable narrative contains names and dates.

feedback.text: Correct. An unexpectedly precise claim about a poorly documented object is the thing to distrust first.

answer.text: Specificity indicates the model retrieved the details from a catalogue during generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No retrieval occurs; the detail is predicted, not looked up.

answer.text: Specificity means the claim can be trusted, since vague output signals uncertainty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is exactly the inference the section warns against.

answer.text: Specificity suggests the temperature was set too low.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low temperature increases predictability, not fabrication of detail.

name.text: 20 Question: The Subtle One: Confidence the Source Never Had

questiontext.text: Your source says “approximately 30 lines” and the AI writes writtenLines="30". Why does this matter beyond tidiness?

generalfeedback.text: Models convert hedged evidence into precise assertions — ranges into years, maybes into counts — producing valid markup that claims more than the source ever did.

answer.text: Downstream work queries these fields as data, and a false precision is worse than a recorded uncertainty because it cannot be seen or undone.

feedback.text: Correct. Module 07's collation will read these values as if they were measurements.

answer.text: Because the schema requires approximate values to use notBefore and notAfter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those attributes are for dates, and the schema does not mandate them here.

answer.text: Because 30 is likely to be the wrong number in most manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It may well be right; the problem is asserting certainty the source withheld.

answer.text: Because TEI forbids numeric attributes on layout elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI provides exactly such attributes.

name.text: 21 Question: The Subtle One: What Is Not There

questiontext.text: Why can an omission never be found by reading the AI file on its own?

generalfeedback.text: Omissions produce no error and cannot be found by reading the AI file alone, so audit by walking your own header element by element.

answer.text: There is nothing to see: no error fires, the structure is clean, and only comparison with your own header reveals the gap.

feedback.text: Correct. A schema judges what you gave it and has no view of what should have been there.

answer.text: Because omissions are always in elements the schema treats as optional.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whether optional or not, an absent element cannot announce itself.

answer.text: Because the model deletes the corresponding element from your file as well.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your file is untouched; the omission is only in the model's output.

answer.text: Because Schematron reports omissions as warnings rather than errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No rule fires at all when nothing invalid was written.

name.text: 22 Question: The Subtle One: The Link That Goes Somewhere Else

questiontext.text: Which kind of fabricated identifier is most dangerous, and what is the only test for it?

generalfeedback.text: Fabricated identifiers most often resolve to a real but wrong record, passing every automatic check, so the only test is following each link and reading what opens.

answer.text: One that is correctly formatted and resolves to a real but wrong record; the only test is following the link and reading what opens.

feedback.text: Correct. It passes valid XML, valid schema, and a resolvable URL, so nothing automatic will flag it.

answer.text: One that resolves to nothing, because a dead link breaks the edition for every reader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A dead link is honest: anyone who clicks discovers the problem immediately.

answer.text: One with an invalid character in the URI, since it will fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a structural error the schema catches for you.

answer.text: One that omits the ref attribute entirely, since the link is then untraceable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is an omission, not a fabricated identifier.

name.text: 23 Question: The Subtle One: The Citation That Does Not Resolve

questiontext.text: Why is a fabricated persistent identifier worse than no identifier at all?

generalfeedback.text: Generated identifiers are correctly shaped and frequently point at the wrong object, so every one must be resolved and read before you commit it.

answer.text: A persistent identifier promises to resolve indefinitely, so a well-formed one pointing at the wrong object is a broken promise that looks like a kept one.

feedback.text: Correct. An ARK off by a character, or a call number in a series that does not exist, fails only when someone follows it.

answer.text: Because an invalid identifier causes the file to fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A correctly shaped identifier validates whether or not it resolves to the right object.

answer.text: Because identifiers cannot be corrected once committed to Git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They can be corrected; the difficulty is that nobody realizes they are wrong.

answer.text: Because fabricated identifiers consume names that real objects need.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The identifier space is not exhaustible in that way.

name.text: 24 Question: Sorting the Differences, and What the Pattern Shows

questiontext.text: Model accuracy tracks how much has been written about a subject. What is the scholarly consequence for cataloguing?

generalfeedback.text: Classify every difference, name precision and recall from your own counts, and state the pattern — structural errors where the schema could reach, invented specifics where only the object could answer.

answer.text: The tool performs worst where the backlog is largest, so unaudited automation widens the gap between well-described and neglected traditions.

feedback.text: Correct. The failure is invisible, because the prose is equally polished whether or not it is accurate.

answer.text: Processing is slower for less-documented traditions, raising the cost per record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The consequence is confident invention, not slower processing.

answer.text: The model declines to describe material it has seen little of.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not decline; it produces fluent output with far more of it invented.

answer.text: The problem is solved by photographing those collections at higher resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deficit is in textual training data, not image quality.

name.text: 25 Question: From Counts to a Defensible Claim

questiontext.text: You have two counts: the raw schema error count and how many of the six fields were wrong or invented. What turns them into the kind of finding the comparison is graded on?

generalfeedback.text: Convert your counts into a specific, checkable claim that separates structural from factual performance and explains why those fields in particular failed.

answer.text: A specific, checkable claim that separates structural from factual performance, names the specific field and error, and explains why those fields in particular failed.

feedback.text: Correct. A marker must be able to check the claim against your files; otherwise it is an impression rather than a finding.

answer.text: A general statement that the AI made several errors, which is unfalsifiable and describes every AI output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the weak example the section rejects: it neither separates structural from factual performance nor names anything specific.

answer.text: A tally of the structural errors the schema caught, since those are the errors you can prove.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structural errors are the cheap findings the machine already announced; they say nothing about what only you can catch.

answer.text: A reflection on how much effort you put into building the dossier, framed as a diary of the week.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The section's third test asks whether the sentence says something about the machine rather than about your own effort.

name.text: 26 Question: Recording the Machine's Part in the File

questiontext.text: Why record the model's version and date in respStmt and revisionDesc?

generalfeedback.text: Record AI contributions in `respStmt` and `revisionDesc` with model versions and dates, because algorithmic provenance is provenance.

answer.text: A future reader must be able to tell which claims came from an editor who examined the object and which from a system predicting text.

feedback.text: Correct. “An AI wrote this” means little in ten years; a version and a date can be checked.

answer.text: Because the schema will not validate an AI-drafted file without a respStmt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require it; the obligation is scholarly.

answer.text: Because publishers require an AI disclaimer on digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is provenance recorded in the file, not a legal disclaimer.

answer.text: Because it allows the AI contribution to be excluded from peer review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It makes the contribution reviewable rather than exempt.

name.text: 27 Question: Friday's Lab, Step by Step

questiontext.text: Why does the lab have you look up your own document's authority identifiers BEFORE prompting the model?

generalfeedback.text: Verify identifiers before prompting, record the untouched output and its first error count, then score six fields and follow every link the model produced.

answer.text: So you hold verified values the model cannot influence, giving you an independent standard to audit its identifiers against.

feedback.text: Correct. Looking them up afterwards risks anchoring your search on what the model already asserted.

answer.text: Because the prompt will not function unless identifiers are included in it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model will generate output regardless; the concern is independence.

answer.text: Because the authority registers are unavailable later in the day.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Availability is not the reason for the ordering.

answer.text: Because the schema requires all identifiers to be present before validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require these identifiers at all.

name.text: 28 Question: Writing the Comparison

questiontext.text: Your evidence shows the schema catching structural errors and missing every subtle one. How should the comparison argue for deterministic validation, and what content actually earns the marks?

generalfeedback.text: The comparison reports method and figures briefly, spends its length on two verified subtle hallucinations, and argues the schema's necessity from your own numbers. Name two specific schema-valid falsehoods, supply your counts, and explain why those fields failed — specificity about your own files is what the mark rewards.

answer.text: Argue from your own numbers that validation removes an entire class of failure at no cost, freeing attention for two subtle hallucinations you name specifically, with the field, the false value, and evidence that they passed validation.

feedback.text: Correct. The schema's necessity is argued from your counts, and credit goes to specific schema-valid falsehoods rather than to a general account of AI limits.

answer.text: Argue that the schema catches most hallucinations and remains the primary safeguard, and report the structural errors it caught as your findings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your own evidence contradicts that claim, and the errors the schema caught are cheap findings every student will have.

answer.text: Argue that better prompts will eventually remove the need for auditing, and spend the word count on the ethics of machine cataloguing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No prompt removes the need for independent verification, and the rubric grades your audit rather than your position on machine cataloguing.

answer.text: Argue that validation matters mainly because Moodle requires valid XML on import, and describe the model's general limitations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Import validity is a technical convenience rather than a methodological argument, and a general account of AI limits reproduces what the lesson already supplied.

name.text: 29 Question: Where This Method Transfers

questiontext.text: Which part of this three-step method transfers beyond TEI headers?

generalfeedback.text: The method — independent ground truth, generation, comparison against truth rather than plausibility, classification of differences — transfers to any structured output a model produces about real objects.

answer.text: The sequence: establish ground truth independently, generate, compare against truth rather than plausibility, and classify the differences.

feedback.text: Correct. That pattern works wherever a model produces structured output about real objects.

answer.text: The specific TEI elements and schema used in this module.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Elements are discipline-specific; the method is what generalises.

answer.text: The prompting technique alone, since better prompts remove the need to audit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No prompt eliminates the need for independent verification.

answer.text: The scorecard's six fields, which apply to any document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The fields are chosen for this assignment; the comparison discipline is the transferable part.

name.text: 30 Question: The Three-Step Cycle, Completed

questiontext.text: What does each step of the three-step cycle contribute that the others cannot, and why does machine generation make schemas more necessary rather than less?

generalfeedback.text: Manual authorship gives truth without scale, schema validation gives structure without truth, and machine generation gives scale without either — the audit is what makes the combination defensible. Generative AI makes deterministic schemas and human editorial judgement more necessary, because automating the cheap errors is what frees attention for the ones only a person can catch.

answer.text: Manual authorship gives truth without scale, schema validation gives structure without truth, and machine generation gives scale without either; automating away the cheap errors is what frees a person's attention for the ones only a person can catch.

feedback.text: Correct. Each step exists because the previous one is insufficient, and only the combination plus the human comparison produces a record you can defend.

answer.text: Manual authorship is the fastest step, the schema makes it reliable, and generation becomes authoritative once its output validates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-authoring is the slowest step, validation certifies construction and never truth, and validating output does not make it authoritative.

answer.text: The schema checks the facts while the model supplies the structure, so generation makes schemas less necessary as models improve.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This inverts both roles, and the argument runs the other way: errors removed automatically leave attention for the expensive ones.

answer.text: Each step replaces the one before it, so a validated AI header no longer needs the hand-authored baseline.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each step exists because the previous one is insufficient; without Tuesday's ground truth you cannot audit what the machine produced.
